questions.q: According to this lesson, what should drive schema design decisions first?
options: Whichever field types are fastest to create
The actual business process the schema needs to represent
The number of objects already in the org
Which objects look the most interesting to build
questions.explain: A well-designed schema is a direct translation of how the business already works, not a collection of objects chosen because they seemed useful.

questions.q: Before creating a new custom object, what does this lesson recommend checking first?
options: Whether Schema Builder has room to display it
Whether the object name is available
Whether a Roll-Up Summary field could replace it
Whether a standard object, possibly with a Record Type or custom fields, already fits
questions.explain: Reusing a standard object, narrowed with a Record Type or extended with a few custom fields, avoids unnecessary schema to document and secure.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call picking a relationship type a decision with real consequences, not just vocabulary?
options: Because only Lookup relationships can be converted to Master-Detail at any time
Because relationship type has no actual effect on data
Because, for example, Master-Detail cascades deletes and locks in sharing in ways that are hard to undo later
Because relationship types affect font size in reports
questions.explain: Master-Detail's cascading delete and inherited sharing are real structural consequences — picking it casually for convenience (like enabling a Roll-Up Summary) can cause problems much later.

questions.q: In Schema Builder, what does an object with relationship lines fanning out to a dozen other objects potentially signal?
options: That the org has exceeded its field limit
That the object needs a Record Type
That the object must be deleted immediately
Either a genuinely central concept, or unrelated concerns bolted onto one object that should be modeled separately
questions.explain: Dense fan-out is fine for a naturally central object like User, but on a less central object it's a warning sign worth investigating.

questions.q: Why does this lesson stress deciding a naming convention early, rather than fixing it later?
options: Because field names cannot be changed after creation under any circumstance
Because naming has no real impact on a schema
Because Salesforce bills by field name length
Because renaming later touches every formula, report, and integration that already references the old name
questions.explain: Inconsistent names cost real time once reports and formulas depend on them, and renaming later means updating everything that already references the old name.
